by cell")] L --> K["Stream"] --> H[("Location history")] R["Rider app"] --> RS["Ride service"] RS --> M["Matching service"] M --> G M --> T[("Trips DB")] RS -- push --> D ``` #### Geospatial index concepts - Geohash: encode a latitude and longitude into a string; nearby places share a prefix. Use a precision where a cell is roughly the search radius. To search, look in the rider's cell and the eight neighbouring cells, then filter by exact distance. - Quadtree: recursively split areas that hold too many drivers. Dense cities get small cells, rural areas big ones. - Other cell systems (hexagonal grids) exist; the idea is the same: turn "near me" into a few key lookups. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant R as Rider participant RS as Ride service participant M as Matching participant G as Geo index participant D as Driver R->>RS: request ride RS->>M: find driver M->>G: drivers in nearby cells G-->>M: candidates M->>M: rank by ETA and rating M->>D: offer ride (timeout 15s) D-->>M: accept M-->>RS: matched RS-->>R: driver details ``` #### Deep dive - Partition the index by city or by cell range; each shard owns an area. Drivers near a border are written to both sides or queried across. - Updates replace the old position; remove a driver from the old cell when moving to a new one. Expire stale drivers with a TTL. - Matching: offer to one best driver at a time, with a timeout, rather than broadcasting to many (avoids double acceptance). Make acceptance atomic (conditional update on the driver's state). - Trip state machine: requested, matched, arrived, in progress, completed, cancelled. Stored durably; location tracking during the trip goes through the stream. - ETA and routing use a maps service; cache common routes. - Surge pricing: supply and demand counts per cell, computed periodically. - Reduce traffic: drivers send less often when idle or stationary, and batch updates when the network is bad. #### Bottlenecks Update rate, hot cells (stadium after a match), and the matching race conditions. #### Trade-offs Accuracy of position versus battery and bandwidth. Geohash is simple but cell edges and varying density cause quirks; quadtree adapts better but is harder to distribute. #### What I would improve Batched global matching for better fleet efficiency, predictive positioning of drivers, and regional deployment. **Interview tip:** Explain "near me" as nine cell lookups, then filter. It turns a hard spatial problem into a key-value problem.

questions.question: System design: how would you design a metrics and monitoring system?
questions.answer:
**Short answer:** Agents collect metrics from services and send them through an ingestion pipeline into a time-series database. A query layer feeds dashboards, and an alert evaluator runs rules and sends notifications. The design must handle huge write volume, control cardinality, downsample old data, and stay up when everything else is failing. #### Requirements - Collect metrics (counters, gauges, histograms) from thousands of hosts and services; dashboards; alerts with routing and silencing; retention of months to years. - Non-functional: very high write rate, queries on recent data in under a second, high availability for alerting, bounded cost. #### Estimates - 10,000 hosts, 200 metrics each, one point every 10 seconds is 200,000 points per second. A point stored compressed is a few bytes, so roughly 20 to 50 GB per day at full resolution. - Alert rules: 20,000 rules evaluated every minute is about 330 evaluations per second. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Agents and SDKs"] --> I["Ingestion gateways"] --> K["Queue"] --> W["Writers"] --> TS[("Time-series DB
sharded by series")] TS --> DS["Downsampler"] --> LT[("Long-term store")] Q["Query service"] --> TS Q --> LT DASH["Dashboards"] --> Q AL["Alert evaluator"] --> Q AL --> RT["Alert router"] --> ON["On-call: pager, chat"] ``` #### API ```text POST /v1/metrics/write batch of {name, labels, timestamp, value} GET /v1/query?expr=rate(http_errors[5m])&from=...&to=... POST /v1/alerts/rules { "expr": "...", "for": "5m", "severity": "page" } ``` #### Data model A series is identified by name plus labels. Points are (timestamp, value). Data is partitioned by series hash and time block. An inverted index maps label values to series, to answer "all series where service=checkout". #### Deep dive - Push versus pull: pull (scrape) makes it easy to know a target is down and to control rate; push suits short-lived jobs and devices behind firewalls. Many systems support both. - Queue buffer: absorbs bursts and lets writers batch. Back pressure and sampling rules protect the store. - Cardinality control: limit the number of label values per metric, reject or drop series that explode. High-cardinality data belongs in logs and traces. - Storage: write-ahead log, in-memory head block, periodic compaction to compressed blocks. - Downsampling: 10-second data for a week, 1-minute for a month, 1-hour for a year. - Alert evaluation: rules run on a schedule against the store. Use "for" durations to avoid flapping, group alerts, deduplicate and route by team and severity, support silences and maintenance windows. - Reliability of the monitor: it must not depend on what it watches. Run it in a separate failure domain, add a "dead man's switch" alert that fires when the monitoring pipeline itself goes quiet, and keep alert evaluation independent of the dashboard query path. #### Bottlenecks Write throughput, high-cardinality queries, expensive dashboards (cache and pre-aggregate with recording rules). #### Trade-offs Full resolution everywhere is expensive; downsampling loses detail. Central versus per-team instances: central is easy to search, per-team limits blast radius. #### What I would improve Anomaly detection, SLO burn-rate alerts, exemplars linking metrics to traces, and multi-region query federation. **Interview tip:** Mention the monitoring-the-monitor problem; it shows operational maturity.

questions.question: System design: how would you design a ticket or seat booking system?
questions.answer:
**Short answer:** The core problem is two people trying to buy the same seat. Use a temporary hold (a reservation with an expiry) created by an atomic conditional update, then confirm after payment. Use optimistic concurrency or row-level locks on the seat, not application-level checks, and handle very high demand with a waiting room. #### Requirements - Browse events and seat maps, select seats, hold them for a few minutes, pay, receive tickets. - Non-functional: no double booking (strong consistency on seat state), fairness under a rush, resilient when payments are slow. #### Estimates - A popular event: 50,000 seats, 1 million people arriving in the first minute. That is a read storm on the seat map and a contention storm on a small number of rows. #### API ```text GET /v1/events/{id}/seats -> map with availability (slightly stale is fine) POST /v1/holds { "event_id": "e1", "seat_ids": ["A12","A13"] } -> hold id, expires_at POST /v1/bookings { "hold_id": "h7", "payment_token": "..." } ``` ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Available Available --> Held: hold request wins Held --> Available: hold expires Held --> Booked: payment succeeds Booked --> [*] ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR U["Users"] --> WR["Waiting room
admit N per minute"] --> G["API"] G --> C[("Seat map cache")] G --> S["Booking service"] S --> DB[("Seats DB")] S --> P["Payment service"] S --> J["Expiry job"] --> DB S --> OB["Outbox: tickets, email"] ``` #### Data model `seats(event_id, seat_id, status, held_by, hold_expires_at, version)`; `bookings(id, user, event_id, seats, status)`. #### Deep dive - Hold with a conditional update: ```sql UPDATE seats SET status = 'HELD', held_by = :user, hold_expires_at = now() + interval '5 minutes' WHERE event_id = :e AND seat_id = :s AND (status = 'AVAILABLE' OR (status = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at < now())); -- affected rows = 1 means you got the seat; 0 means someone else did ``` - Several seats: do it in one transaction in a fixed order (sorted seat ids) to avoid deadlocks, and roll back if any seat fails. - Options: pessimistic locking (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) is simple for low contention; optimistic version checks avoid long locks; a distributed lock is rarely necessary if the database enforces the rule. - Expiry: a background job or lazy check returns expired holds to availability. - Seat map reads: served from a cache that can be a few seconds stale; the hold step is the source of truth. Push seat changes to viewers over SSE if desired. - Rush: waiting room (virtual queue) limits how many users enter the booking flow; the rest see their position. This protects the database and is fairer than a crash. - Payment: after a successful payment, confirm the booking in a transaction; if payment succeeds but the hold expired, refund or re-check. Use idempotency keys. - Bots: rate limits, captchas, per-account limits. #### Bottlenecks The few hottest rows or events, the database during the first minute, and payment timeouts leaving holds stuck. #### Trade-offs Longer holds are friendlier but reduce availability for others. General admission (no seat choice) is simpler: a counter with a conditional decrement. #### What I would improve Dynamic hold length, better bot defence, and per-section sharding. **Interview tip:** Say "the database enforces the rule with an atomic conditional update; the cache is only for display".

questions.question: System design: how would you design an API gateway?
questions.answer:
**Short answer:** An API gateway is a stateless, horizontally scaled reverse proxy that terminates TLS, authenticates the caller, applies rate limits, routes to backend services using a route table, and emits metrics and traces. Keep the data path thin and fast, and keep configuration in a control plane that pushes changes to the gateway nodes. #### Requirements - Route requests to many services, authenticate (JWT, API keys, mutual TLS), rate limit and enforce quotas, transform requests lightly, cache selected responses, and log. - Non-functional: very low added latency (a few ms), very high availability (it is in front of everything), config changes without restarts, safe rollouts. #### Estimates - 50,000 requests per second at peak, 5 ms budget per request. A single well-written gateway node handles thousands of requests per second, so about 10 to 20 nodes with headroom across zones. ```mermaid flowchart LR C["Clients"] --> LB["L4 load balancer"] --> G["Gateway nodes"] G --> S1["Service A"] G --> S2["Service B"] G --> S3["Service C"] CP["Control plane
routes, policies, keys"] -- config push --> G G --> R[("Redis: rate limits")] G --> O["Metrics, logs, traces"] G --> ID["Identity provider
public keys cached"] ``` #### API (control plane) ```text PUT /v1/routes/orders { "match": "/orders/*", "upstream": "orders.svc", "auth": "jwt", "rate": "100/min" } ``` ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant C as Client participant G as Gateway participant R as Rate limiter participant S as Service C->>G: request with token G->>G: terminate TLS, validate JWT locally G->>R: check limit R-->>G: allowed G->>S: forward with trace id and user headers S-->>G: response G-->>C: response ``` #### Deep dive - Plugin pipeline: ordered filters (auth, rate limit, transform, cache, log). Keep each fast and bounded. Run user code carefully (sandbox, timeouts). - Auth: validate JWT signatures locally using cached public keys, so no network call per request. Pass identity downstream in trusted headers, and strip any client-supplied identity headers. - Routing: a trie or radix tree of paths in memory; upstream selection with health checks, retries (idempotent only), timeouts and circuit breaking. - Config distribution: control plane stores routes in a database, nodes subscribe or poll and swap the route table atomically. Validate before activating, and keep the last good config if the new one is broken. - Rollouts: canary and weighted routing for services (95 percent old, 5 percent new). - Resilience: stateless nodes, spread across zones, autoscale on CPU and connections. Fail open or closed deliberately when auth or limiter dependencies fail. - Protocols: HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSocket upgrades, request and response size limits, timeouts for slow clients. - Security: WAF rules, schema validation, IP allow lists, mutual TLS to backends. #### Bottlenecks Connection count, TLS handshakes (session reuse, offload), plugin latency, and the gateway becoming a place for business logic. #### Trade-offs Centralised gateway gives consistent policy but is a shared dependency and a possible bottleneck. A service mesh moves some of this to sidecars for east-west traffic. Use both: gateway for north-south, mesh for service-to-service. #### What I would improve Per-tenant isolation of noisy neighbours, request replay tools, and a developer portal with API keys and usage analytics. **Interview tip:** Distinguish control plane from data plane; it is the idea that makes the design scalable and safe to change.

questions.question: System design: how would you design typeahead or autocomplete at scale?
questions.answer:
**Short answer:** Precompute the top suggestions for every prefix from query logs, store them in a fast in-memory or key-value structure, and serve each keystroke with one lookup. Update the data periodically with a pipeline, and combine global popularity with recency and light personalisation. The client debounces and caches to cut traffic. #### Requirements - As a user types, return the top 5 to 10 completions within about 100 ms. - Rank by popularity and freshness, support multiple languages, filter inappropriate suggestions, optionally personalise. #### Estimates - 10 million daily users, 10 searches each, about 5 keystroke requests per search is 500 million requests per day, about 6,000 per second average and 20,000 at peak. - Distinct prefixes: a few hundred million. Storing 10 suggestions each at about 100 bytes is tens of gigabytes. It fits in memory across a few nodes, or in a key-value store with a cache. #### API ```text GET /v1/suggest?q=how+to+c&limit=8&lang=en -> { "suggestions": ["how to cook rice", "how to create a resume", ...] } ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR U["User keystrokes"] --> CL["Client: debounce and local cache"] --> CDN["CDN or edge cache"] --> SS["Suggest service"] SS --> MEM[("Prefix store
prefix to top-K list")] L["Search logs"] --> A["Aggregation job
counts per query"] --> B["Builder
make top-K per prefix"] --> MEM F["Filter lists and blocklist"] --> B ``` The online path is a single read. All heavy work is offline. #### Data model - Trie view: each node stores the top K completions below it (with scores). A lookup walks the prefix and returns the stored list; no subtree scan. - Flattened form: key-value, `prefix -> [(query, score), ...]`. Easier to shard and cache than a pointer-based trie. - Score: weighted count with time decay, so trending queries rise and old ones fall. ```mermaid flowchart TD R["root"] --> H["h"] H --> HO["ho"] HO --> HOW["how: top 8 stored here"] HOW --> HOWT["how t: top 8 stored here"] ``` #### Deep dive - Building: log pipeline aggregates query counts per hour. A builder merges recent counts with long-term counts, then writes a new snapshot. Swap atomically. A weekly full rebuild plus frequent incremental updates is common. - Freshness: breaking news needs a fast path. Use a small real-time trending layer (a stream job over the last few minutes) and merge it at query time. - Sharding: by prefix (first one or two characters), noting that some prefixes (such as "s") are much heavier; split by more characters or by hash. - Caching: browser caches by prefix, CDN caches popular prefixes for seconds to minutes, and the service keeps hot prefixes in memory. - Short prefixes (1 to 2 characters) are the hottest and least useful; precompute and cache them aggressively. - Typos: fuzzy matching via edit distance on a limited candidate set, as a later improvement. - Personalisation: merge a user's recent searches into the list; keep it separate and small. - Safety: filter offensive, private or legally risky suggestions in the builder, with a fast blocklist hotfix path. #### Bottlenecks Memory of the prefix store, hot short prefixes, and the delay between a trend starting and appearing. #### Trade-offs Precomputed lists are fast but slightly stale. A search-engine index with edge n-grams is flexible but costs more per query. Larger K improves coverage but increases memory. #### What I would improve Learning-to-rank, context-aware suggestions (language, location, device), and A/B testing of ranking. **Interview tip:** Say "one lookup per keystroke, all computation offline", and mention debouncing on the client.

questions.question: How do you recover when you get stuck in a system design interview, and what are the common pitfalls?
questions.answer:
**Short answer:** Stay calm, say what you are stuck on, return to requirements and the simplest design that works, and ask the interviewer for a hint without shame. Interviewers value recovery and reasoning more than a perfect answer. Most failures come from avoidable habits: no structure, no numbers, over-engineering, and ignoring trade-offs. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Stuck"] --> B["Say it aloud:
where exactly am I stuck?"] B --> C["Restate requirements
and numbers"] C --> D["Propose the simplest design that works"] D --> E["List its weaknesses"] E --> F["Fix the biggest one
or ask for a hint"] ``` **Recovery moves** - Narrate: "I am between a queue and a direct call; let me compare them against our latency goal." - Go simpler: a single server and one database. Then scale the part that fails the numbers. - Pick an option and state the trade-off, rather than waiting for a perfect answer. Say you can revisit it. - Ask: "Would you like me to go deeper on storage or on delivery?" The interviewer often points to what matters. - Use a known pattern: cache, queue, shard, replicate, CDN. Ask which constraint each one relaxes. - If you made an error, correct it openly and move on. Calm correction is a strong signal. **Common pitfalls** | Pitfall | Better habit | | --- | --- | | Starting to draw before clarifying | Spend the first minutes on requirements and scope | | No numbers | Make rough estimates and use them to decide | | Name-dropping tools (Kafka, Cassandra) with no reason | Explain the need first, then the tool | | Over-engineering for a small problem | Start simple, scale where numbers demand it | | Ignoring failures | Ask "what if this dies?" for each box | | Silent thinking | Think aloud; the interviewer cannot score what they cannot hear | | Only the happy path | Cover retries, duplicates, ordering, hot keys | | Depth on the wrong part | Check in, and follow the interviewer's interest | | Defensive about feedback | Treat challenges as collaboration | | Running out of time | Keep a clock: requirements, design, deep dive, wrap-up | **For a lead-level interview, also show** - Operations: monitoring, rollout, on-call, cost. - Team and delivery: what you would build first, how to phase the work, how to de-risk. - Decision records: you can explain why, and what would make you change. **Interview tip:** Practise aloud with a timer on five classic problems, record yourself, and review the pauses. Fluency under pressure comes from repeating the framework until it is automatic.
